Basics of the Game Introduction In TEKKEN – The Board Game, you step into intense head-to-head battles where every choice matters. Each opponent is unique, with a distinct fighting style, but the core rules apply to all. Your goal is simple – reduce your rival’s HP to zero – yet the path to victory is shaped by sharp thinking, reading your opponent, and precise timing. On your turn, you will either: Predict which attack your opponent is about to unleash and counter it. Choose one of the three cards in your hand, play it face-down, and try to catch your opponent off guard. It may sound like guessing, but this is far from random. Skilled players piece together clues: the combos an opponent might trigger, their position on the Stage, extensions from their previous cards, how many cards remain in their deck, and the current HP of both fighters. These details – and many more you’ll discover with experience – separate victory from defeat. Those who learn to read the fight will win more often, making this a true competitive game. You can jump in and play right away, even with little experience, much like “button-mashing” in the video game. But the real satisfaction comes when you master the flow – chaining attacks into powerful combos, setting traps, and playing your cards in the perfect sequence. This is not a random guessing game. It’s a duel of wits, reflexes, and adaptability – a tactical fight where anticipation and insight decide the outcome. Goal of the Game Defeat your opponent by reducing their HP (Health Points) to zero, thus winning the Round. By default you win the game when you win three rounds. In TEKKEN – The Board Game — a fighting tabletop game that translates the dynamic and tactical experience of the TEKKEN video game series — two unique characters fight in one of various stages, using different attacks and performing spectacular combos.

A unique card-driven duel system ensures that every character retains their signature playstyle, while custom decks, combos, heat, and the "rage moves" system add layers of tactical depth, challenging you to manage your hand of cards to move across the board, attack your enemy, and ensure they can't anticipate your next move. Combine cards in the correct order to create an epic combo, activate your special moves, and use the stage special rules like wall break, floor break, and wall blast to your advantage.

The base mode works for 1-2 players, but the game also has a tournament mode for 1-8 players.

—description from the publisher

The price is justified by the detailed miniatures, which are, however, overproduced for pure gameplay.  Even though all the expansions add a few characters, the replayability and asymmetry are very poor, as some characters feel dry and, above all, the same.  Street Masters is the better game in every respect, and costs about the same in the all-inclusive version. [Rating: 2/10] Just a bad bad game. I can't believe how much this game sold. Josh hated it also. A big board and movement doesn't matter. Just cant predict anything. Way better fighting games out there.

[Rating: 2/10] PROS  - Cool colors, punish mechanic if the game wasn't the closest thing to RPS I have ever played  CONS  - Oh boy....so many (art is lazy, design is lazy, core loop feels so luck based (you can deduce when someone shouldn't play a high if they are 2 spaces away...I think that's all), movement feels weird and uneventful, all cards being the same is lazy)  - This feels like a true IP cash grab to me. I can't believe this raised almost 900k on gamefound.  MEMORABLE MOMENTS  - Kevin almost instakilling me on first turn of last round

[Rating: 2.5/10] 2 games played, 1:1 score. Didn't care enough about the game to break the tie. Too random, too simple, too uninteresting. Just... Boring. Despite the excitement of the guy teaching us the game, we just didn't get any of his hype. Disappointing. Lacks meaningful choice. Can be over in two rounds with no real way of defending.  Took RPS design from fighting games too literally.  Could just be issues with the prototype that get ironed out, but I wasn't this disappointed in a game in a long time.

[Rating: 3/10] Just not much going on here. Boring rock paper scissors game that's been made to sell minis. The only semblance of strategy comes from managing the arena mechanics and card counting.  There is, in theory, some cool ideas here. The various combos and characters could be fun if combined with a compelling game system, because they are satisfying. Zero interest in ever playing this though, unless it was to entertain a younger relative or something.  On top of that it's $140 CAD + shipping for the core set. Wild. Kickstarter board game culture in a nutshell. Subtracted an extra point for value prop

[Rating: 3/10] „Choose one of the three cards in your hand, play it face-down, and try to catch your opponent off guard. It may sound like guessing, but this is far from random.”  Yeah, tell that to someone who lost just because their opponent made correct guesses even when there was absolutely no hint to what he was about to do. Frustrating is an understatement.

[Rating: 4/10] Tried out the game and I like how simple it is, but found the theme to be lacking too much.   Would definitely play my buddies' copy of the game, but was ultimately let down.
